title: Pileći paprikaš with noodles
description: Chicken stewed slowly with lots of onion and sweet paprika, finished with sour cream. Served over wide noodles, the Slavonian way.

steps.text: Cut the chicken legs into thighs and drumsticks at the joint and pat them dry. Chop the onions finely and dice the pepper.
steps.tip: Cut where the leg bends: the knife slides through the joint easily there.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pot on medium-high and brown the chicken for 8 minutes, turning, until golden. Take it out.
steps.tip: Golden skin gives the sauce its flavour. Do not crowd the pot.

steps: Turn the heat to medium-low and fry the onions in the same pot for 12 minutes until soft and golden. Add the pepper for the last few minutes.

steps.text: Take the pot off the heat and stir in the paprika and tomato paste. Put the chicken back with its juices and add the salt, pepper and {600 ml} water.
steps.tip: Paprika burns easily, which is why it goes in off the heat.

steps.text: Bring to a simmer, cover and cook gently for 35 minutes, until the meat comes away from the bone.
steps.tip: Shake the pot now and then so nothing sticks.

steps.text: Whisk the sour cream with the flour and a ladle of the hot sauce until smooth. Stir it into the pot and simmer for 3 minutes until thickened.
steps.tip: Mixing it with hot sauce first stops the sour cream splitting into flecks.

steps.text: Meanwhile cook the noodles in salted water as the packet says. Serve the paprikaš over the noodles.
steps.tip: It keeps 3 days. Reheat it gently, without boiling.

title: Podvarak (pork baked on sauerkraut)
description: Thick slices of pork neck baked slowly on sauerkraut with bacon and onion, with boiled potatoes. A winter Sunday classic from the north.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 180 °C. Taste the sauerkraut: if it is very sour or salty, rinse it briefly and squeeze it out. Slice the onions and dice the bacon.
steps.tip: Some sourness is the point of podvarak, so rinse only if it is really strong. The sauerkraut and bacon bring most of the salt.

steps: Melt the lard in a large ovenproof pot or deep roasting dish on medium heat. Fry the bacon and onions for 8 minutes until soft and golden.
Add the sauerkraut, paprika, pepper and bay leaves and stir well. Pour in {200 ml} water.

steps.text: Cut the pork into thick slices, season them with the salt and lay them on top of the sauerkraut.
steps.tip: Pork neck stays juicy in a long bake. Leaner cuts dry out.

steps.text: Cover with a lid or foil and bake for 1 hour. Then uncover and bake for 30 minutes more, until the meat is browned on top and very tender.
steps.tip: Check halfway: if the sauerkraut looks dry, add a splash of water. It should be juicy, not swimming.

steps: Meanwhile peel the potatoes, cut them into chunks and boil them in salted water for 20 minutes until soft. Drain.

steps.text: Serve the pork on the sauerkraut with the potatoes.
steps.tip: Like sarma, it tastes even better the next day. It keeps 4 days in the fridge.

title: Hake na bijelo (with potatoes and garlic)
description: White fish and potatoes shaken with garlic, parsley and plenty of olive oil into a rough, creamy mash. A quick everyday take on Christmas Eve bakalar.
steps: Peel the potatoes and slice them about 1 cm thick. Chop the garlic and parsley finely.
Put the potatoes in a wide pot, just cover them with water, add the bay leaves and half the salt and bring to the boil. Simmer for 12 minutes, until almost soft.

steps.text: Cut the hake into large pieces, season with the rest of the salt and lay it on top of the potatoes. Cover and simmer gently for 8 minutes, until the fish turns white and flakes.
steps.tip: Frozen hake works well. Thaw it in the fridge overnight first. Fresh cod is good too.

steps.text: Pour off most of the water, leaving about a mug in the pot. Take out the bay leaves.
steps.tip: This starchy water turns into the creamy sauce, so do not pour it all away.

steps.text: Add the garlic, parsley, pepper and olive oil. Hold the lid on and shake the pot hard for a minute, until the potatoes and fish break into a creamy, rough mash.
steps.tip: Shaking, not stirring, is the traditional way: it makes it creamy while keeping some chunks.

steps.text: Taste for salt and serve warm, with a little more olive oil on top.
steps.tip: For Christmas Eve, Dalmatians make it with dried bakalar, soaked in water for 2 to 3 days and cooked for hours. Hake gives the same taste on a weeknight.

title: Octopus salad with potatoes
description: Tender boiled octopus with potatoes, onion, parsley, olive oil and vinegar. A Dalmatian summer favourite that gets better the next day.
ahead: move the octopus to the fridge to thaw

ingredients.note: red onion if you have it

steps.text: If the octopus is frozen, thaw it overnight in the fridge.
steps.tip: Freezing makes octopus tender, so frozen is perfect. Fishmongers often freeze fresh octopus for this reason.

steps.text: Put the octopus in a large pot with the bay leaves, cover with cold water and bring to the boil. Do not add salt. Simmer gently, lid on, for 45 to 60 minutes.
steps.tip: It is done when a fork slides easily into the thickest part of a tentacle. Salt in the water can make it tough.

steps: Turn off the heat and let the octopus cool in its water for 15 minutes, then lift it out.
Meanwhile boil the potatoes in their skins in salted water for 20 minutes, until a knife slides in. Peel them while warm and cut into chunks.
Cut the octopus into bite-size pieces. Slice the onion thinly, chop the garlic and parsley and cut the tomatoes into wedges.

steps.text: Mix everything in a big bowl with the olive oil, vinegar, lemon juice, salt and pepper.
steps.tip: Leave it for at least half an hour so the flavours mix. It is even better the next day.

steps.text: Serve at room temperature.
steps.tip: It keeps 2 days in the fridge. Take it out a little before eating.

title: Pan-fried trout with garlic potatoes
description: Whole trout fried crisp in a little flour, with potatoes tossed in garlic, parsley and olive oil. A Gorski kotar and Plitvice favourite.
steps: Peel the potatoes, cut them into chunks and boil them in salted water for 15 minutes until soft. Drain.

steps.text: Rinse the trout and pat them dry inside and out. Season inside and out with half the salt and dust them with the flour.
steps.tip: A thin coat of flour gives crisp skin and stops the fish sticking.

steps.text: Heat {3 tbsp} of the olive oil in a large frying pan on medium-high. Fry the trout two at a time for 5 to 6 minutes on each side until golden and cooked through.
steps.tip: It is done when the flesh comes off the backbone easily. Turn the fish only once, carefully, with a wide spatula.

steps: Meanwhile chop the garlic and parsley. Warm most of the rest of the oil with the garlic in the potato pot for 1 minute, then add the potatoes, parsley and the rest of the salt and toss.
Wash and tear the lettuce and dress it with the vinegar, a pinch of salt and the last of the oil.
Serve the trout with the garlic potatoes, the salad and lemon wedges.

title: Stuffed zucchini in tomato sauce
description: Zucchini halves filled with meat and rice, baked in tomato sauce under a layer of cheese. The summer cousin of punjene paprike.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 190 °C. Cut the zucchini in half lengthways and scoop out the middle with a teaspoon, leaving a 1 cm wall. Chop the scooped flesh and the onion.
steps.tip: Keep the scooped flesh: it goes into the sauce, so nothing is wasted.

steps: Mix the meat, rice, half the onion, the egg, paprika, {1 tsp} of the salt and the pepper with your hand.

steps.text: Fill the zucchini halves with the meat, pressing gently.
steps.tip: Do not pack it tight, because the rice swells as it cooks.

steps: Heat the oil in a pan and fry the rest of the onion and the chopped zucchini for 5 minutes. Add the passata, the rest of the salt and {200 ml} water, then pour it into a baking dish.
Lay the zucchini in the sauce, filling side up. Cover the dish with foil and bake for 35 minutes.

steps.text: Take off the foil, scatter the grated cheese over and bake for 15 minutes more until golden.
steps.tip: The rice in the filling should be soft. Serve with bread or mashed potatoes. Keeps 3 days.

title: Potato goulash with sausage
description: A big pot of potatoes stewed with paprika, onion and smoked sausage until thick. Cheap, filling and better the next day.
steps: Peel the potatoes and cut them into 3 cm chunks. Chop the onions and garlic, dice the pepper and slice the sausages into rounds.
Heat the oil in a large pot on medium heat. Brown the sausages for 5 minutes and lift them out.
Fry the onions in the same pot for 10 minutes until soft and golden. Add the pepper and garlic for 2 minutes.

steps.text: Take the pot off the heat and stir in the paprika and tomato paste. Add the potatoes, sausages, bay leaves, salt, pepper and {1500 ml} water.
steps.tip: Paprika burns easily, which is why it goes in off the heat.

steps.text: Bring to the boil, then simmer for 25 minutes, stirring now and then, until the potatoes are soft and starting to fall apart.
steps.tip: Crush a few potato chunks against the side of the pot: they thicken the goulash.

steps.text: Taste for salt and serve with bread.
steps.tip: A big pot keeps 3 days and tastes even better reheated.

title: Zagorski štrukli (baked)
description: Thin stretched dough rolled around fresh cheese, cut into pillows and baked in cream until golden. Zagorje's most famous dish.

steps.text: Mix the flour and half the salt in a bowl. Add one egg, the oil and about {200 ml} lukewarm water and knead for 10 minutes into a smooth, soft dough.
steps.tip: It should be softer than pasta dough and not stick to your hands. Add a spoon of water or flour to get there.

steps.text: Divide it into two balls, brush them with a little oil, cover with a bowl and leave to rest for 30 minutes.
steps.tip: Resting relaxes the dough so it stretches thin without tearing.

steps: Meanwhile mix the cottage cheese, the other eggs, half the sour cream and the rest of the salt into a smooth filling. Heat the oven to 200 °C and butter a large baking dish.

steps.text: Spread a clean tablecloth on the table and dust it with flour. Roll one ball out, then stretch it with the backs of your hands into a very thin sheet, until you can almost see through it.
steps.tip: Small holes do not matter. Work from the middle outwards and let the edges hang over the table.

steps.text: Dot half the filling over the sheet. Fold the edges in, then lift the cloth to roll the dough up loosely. Cut the roll into pieces about 8 cm long with the edge of a plate, pressing down to seal the ends.
steps.tip: The edge of a plate seals the pieces as it cuts, so the filling stays inside. This is the traditional way.

steps: Lay the pieces in the dish and repeat with the second ball of dough.

steps.text: Mix the rest of the sour cream with the cooking cream and pour it over. Dot with the butter and bake for 40 to 45 minutes until golden and bubbling.
steps.tip: Serve hot, straight from the dish. Leftovers reheat well in the oven.

title: Lamb and potatoes, peka style
description: Lamb, potatoes and onions slow-roasted covered with wine and rosemary, then uncovered until crisp. The oven version of the Dalmatian peka.

ingredients.note: on the bone, in large pieces

steps.text: Heat the oven to 180 °C. Peel the potatoes and cut them into large chunks. Cut the onions into quarters and slice the garlic.
steps.tip: Ask the butcher to cut the lamb into large pieces for you.

steps: Toss the lamb, potatoes, onions and garlic in a large roasting tin or deep ovenproof pot with the olive oil, rosemary, salt and pepper.

steps.text: Pour in the wine and {200 ml} water. Cover tightly with a lid or two layers of foil.
steps.tip: Under a peka, an iron bell covered with embers, the meat first steams in its own juices, then browns. A tight cover copies that.

steps: Bake covered for 1.5 hours, turning everything once halfway.

steps.text: Uncover, turn the oven up to 220 °C and roast for 30 minutes more, until the lamb and potatoes are browned and crisp at the edges.
steps.tip: The meat is ready when it pulls away from the bone easily.

steps.text: Rest it for 10 minutes, then serve straight from the tin with the juices spooned over and a green salad on the side.
steps.tip: Leftovers keep 3 days. Reheat them in the oven so the potatoes crisp up again.

title: Srdele na savor (marinated sardines)
description: Crisp fried sardines layered with soft onions in a sweet and sour vinegar marinade. An old Dalmatian way of keeping fish, eaten cold with bread.

ingredients.note: for frying, some stays in the pan

steps.text: Clean the sardines: pull off each head, pulling the insides out with it, and rinse under cold water. Pat dry.
steps.tip: Ask at the fish counter to clean them, or buy them cleaned.

steps: Season the sardines with half the salt and toss them in the flour, shaking off the extra.

steps.text: Heat the sunflower oil in a frying pan on medium-high. Fry the sardines in batches for 2 minutes on each side until golden and crisp. Drain them on kitchen paper.
steps.tip: The oil is ready when a pinch of flour sizzles at once. Never leave hot oil alone.

steps: Slice the onions thinly. In another pan, cook them gently in the olive oil for 15 minutes, until soft and sweet but not brown.
Add the vinegar, {100 ml} water, the raisins, bay leaves, sugar, pepper and the rest of the salt and simmer for 5 minutes.
Layer the sardines and the hot onions in a dish, finishing with onions, and pour all the liquid over.

steps.text: Let it cool, cover and leave it in the fridge overnight, or at least for a few hours. Serve cold with bread.
steps.tip: It keeps 4 days in the fridge and tastes better every day.

title: Pašta fažol (bean and pasta soup)
description: A thick Dalmatian soup of beans, small pasta and a little bacon, half way between a soup and a stew. Cheap, filling and warming.

ingredients.note: borlotti if you can find them, drained

steps: Chop the onion, carrot, celeriac and garlic finely and dice the bacon. Drain and rinse the beans.
Heat {2 tbsp} of the olive oil in a large pot on medium heat and fry the bacon for 3 minutes. Add the vegetables and cook for 10 minutes until soft.
Stir in the tomato paste for 1 minute. Add the beans, bay leaves, salt, pepper and {1500 ml} water and simmer for 25 minutes.

steps.text: Take out a mug of beans, mash them with a fork and stir them back in.
steps.tip: This is what makes pašta fažol thick and creamy.

steps.text: Add the pasta and cook for about 10 minutes until soft, stirring now and then so it does not stick.
steps.tip: Add hot water if it gets too thick: it should be halfway between a soup and a stew.

steps.text: Serve with chopped parsley and a drizzle of the rest of the olive oil.
steps.tip: It thickens a lot overnight, so add water when you reheat it. Keeps 3 days.

title: Chicken rižoto with peas
description: The everyday Croatian rižoto: rice cooked with chicken, carrot and peas in stock until moist and creamy, finished with cheese.
steps: Dice the chicken, chop the onion and dice the carrots. Crumble the stock cube into {900 ml} hot water.
Heat the oil in a wide pan with a lid on medium-high and fry the chicken for 5 minutes until white all over. Add the onion and carrot and cook for 5 minutes more.
Add the rice and stir for 1 minute until coated in the oil.

steps.text: Pour in the hot stock, add the pepper and bring to a simmer. Cover and cook on low for 15 minutes, stirring once or twice.
steps.tip: Croatian home rižoto is made this simple way, not ladle by ladle like Italian risotto. The stock cube brings the salt.

steps: Stir in the peas and cook for 3 minutes more, until the rice is soft and most of the liquid has been absorbed.

steps.text: Take the pan off the heat, stir in the grated parmesan and parsley, cover and leave for 2 minutes before serving.
steps.tip: It should be moist, not soupy. Serve with a cabbage or green salad. Keeps 2 days.
